# Comparison of allogeneic vs autologous bone marrow–derived mesenchymal stem cells delivered by transendocardial injection in patients with ischemic cardiomyopathy: the POSEIDON randomized trial.

CONTEXT Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) are under evaluation as a therapy for ischemic cardiomyopathy (ICM). Both autologous and allogeneic MSC therapies are possible; however, their safety and efficacy have not been compared. OBJECTIVE To test whether allogeneic MSCs are as safe and effective as autologous MSCs in patients with left ventricular (LV) dysfunction due to ICM. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PATIENTS A phase 1/2 randomized comparison (POSEIDON study) in a US tertiary-care referral hospital of allogeneic and autologous MSCs in 30 patients with LV dysfunction due to ICM between April 2, 2010, and September 14, 2011, with 13-month follow-up. INTERVENTION Twenty million, 100 million, or 200 million cells (5 patients in each cell type per dose level) were delivered by transendocardial stem cell injection into 10 LV sites. MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES Thirty-day postcatheterization incidence of predefined treatment-emergent serious adverse events (SAEs). Efficacy assessments included 6-minute walk test, exercise peak VO2, Minnesota Living with Heart Failure Questionnaire (MLHFQ), New York Heart Association class, LV volumes, ejection fraction (EF), early enhancement defect (EED; infarct size), and sphericity index. Echocardiographic ARD was studied in 260 consecutive intracranial aneurysm (IA) patients (Jan 2008–Dec 2010). ARD was larger in the "eccentric" group (age <55 with ruptured aneurysm, ≥7 mm aneurysm, or multiple aneurysms) than non-eccentric (P=0.049; multivariable P=0.02); similar in the <55-year subgroup (P=0.03), while hypertension favored non-eccentric (P=0.01). Height was inversely related to aneurysm size (P=0.004). Conclusion: some IA patients share an intrinsic wall defect with aortopathy, possibly from shared neural crest cell origin.

Primary outcome: 30-day treatment-emergent serious adverse events; efficacy included 6-minute walk, peak VO2, MLHFQ, NYHA class, LV volumes, EF, and infarct size.

Smokers with COPD showed increased neutrophils and CD8+ cells within airway smooth muscle compared with non-smokers, suggesting these cells may drive smoking-induced airflow limitation. Investigators examined surgical specimens from 26 thoracotomy subjects—eight smokers with COPD, ten smokers with normal lung function, and eight non-smoking controls—using immunohistochemistry to quantify neutrophils, macrophages, mast cells, and CD4+/CD8+ cells in peripheral airway smooth muscle. Smokers with normal lung function also had neutrophilic infiltration, but to a lesser extent. Across all subjects, neutrophilic infiltration was inversely related to forced expiratory volume in 1 second (% predicted). COPD is an inflammatory disorder of chronic airflow limitation whose link to functional abnormalities remains uncertain, and inflammatory cell–smooth muscle interaction may be crucial. The microlocalisation of neutrophils and CD8+ cells implicates them in the pathogenesis of smoking-induced airflow limitation.

# Role of AMP-activated protein kinase in mechanism of metformin action.

Metformin is a widely used drug for treatment of type 2 diabetes with no defined cellular mechanism of action. Its glucose-lowering effect results from decreased hepatic glucose production and increased glucose utilization. Metformin's beneficial effects on circulating lipids have been linked to reduced fatty liver. AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) is a major cellular regulator of lipid and glucose metabolism. Here we report that metformin activates AMPK in hepatocytes; as a result, acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) activity is reduced, fatty acid oxidation is induced, and expression of lipogenic enzymes is suppressed. Activation of AMPK by metformin or an adenosine analogue suppresses expression of SREBP-1, a key lipogenic transcription factor. In metformin-treated rats, hepatic expression of SREBP-1 (and other lipogenic) mRNAs and protein is reduced; activity of the AMPK target, ACC, is also reduced. Using a novel AMPK inhibitor, we find that AMPK activation is required for metformin's inhibitory effect on glucose production by hepatocytes. In isolated rat skeletal muscles, metformin stimulates glucose uptake coincident with AMPK activation. Activation of AMPK provides a unified explanation for the pleiotropic beneficial effects of this drug; these results also suggest that alternative means of modulating AMPK should be useful for the treatment of metabolic disorders.

CARS (Compensatory Anti-Inflammatory Response Syndrome), proposed by Roger Bone (1997), describes counter-regulatory mechanisms limiting overzealous inflammation in sepsis/SIRS, potentially raising ICU susceptibility to nosocomial infections (per animal 'two-hit' models, procedure-dependent). Circulating leukocytes are reprogrammed, not globally defective; tissue leukocytes are primed/activated rather than immunosuppressed—an adapted, compartmentalized response silencing acute proinflammatory genes while preserving anti-infectious ones. Separately, CAR-redirected Tregs targeting lung epithelia in mouse allergic asthma accumulated in lung and tracheobronchial lymph nodes, reduced airway hyper-reactivity and eosinophilic inflammation, and prevented excessive mucus, allergen-specific IgE and Th2 cytokine rises, outperforming non-modified Tregs—enabling therapy for severe allergic asthma. A third study estimates adverse consequences of unmet need among older dual-eligible versus Medicare-only beneficiaries.
